e.t: Abal, also rendered Aval, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a particular person or place in the Greek LXX text, though the available information does not specify which. This name occurs once in the LXX corpus, at Bel and the Dragon 1:2. Its precise identification depends on the surrounding verse and passage, not on the name itself.

This Greek LXX adjective means “helpless”: lacking the ability, strength, or available help needed to deal with a situation. It describes someone or something left without effective assistance, rather than naming a particular person or event. The word occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings represented here, including Psalms, Wisdom, and 2 Maccabees. Its exact force in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

Adenikam, also rendered Athenikam, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, the Septuagint, it appears once, at Nehemiah 7:18. The name itself identifies a person, but no broader definition is given. Its precise significance in that passage comes from the surrounding verse and list, not from the name alone.

This Greek LXX verb describes treating someone injuriously or plaguing them. It expresses harmful action directed toward another person, rather than a neutral condition or description. Its central meanings are “treat injuriously” and “plague.” The word occurs three times in the deuterocanonical Greek corpus: twice in 2 Maccabees and once in 3 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense consistently points to inflicting harm or distress.

This noun means “glade,” referring to a place associated with trees or woodland. It names a location rather than an action, person, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 42 times across 42 verses, showing that it is a recurring place-word in the biblical landscape. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage and how that location functions there.

This Greek Old Testament verb means “make known again”: to reveal or identify someone or something once more. It describes an act of bringing knowledge into the open, rather than merely possessing or remembering it. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, in Genesis 45:1. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning centers on renewed disclosure or recognition.

This noun means a votive offering: something dedicated or presented in fulfillment of a vow. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both within Deuteronomy 7:26. The word identifies an object given or devoted in a religious setting, rather than describing a person, action, or emotion. Its precise significance in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and its instruction about what may or may not be brought into one’s house.

This word means “renewal”: a making new again or restoring something to fresh strength. It is a noun, so it names the process or result of becoming new rather than describing an action by itself. In the Greek Old Testament tradition, it occurs once, in 1 Maccabees 12:17. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and wider context, which are not included here. The word’s central idea remains renewal—an earlier condition being refreshed, restored, or made new again.

This verb means “bring up” or “carry up,” describing movement of a person or thing toward a higher place or position. Its central idea is upward transfer: something is lifted, brought, or carried from one location to another. The word appears 149 times in the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, so it serves as a recurring action word rather than a rare technical term. Its exact force in any verse depends on what is being moved and the surrounding sentence.

This Greek LXX noun means “live coal,” referring to coal that remains burning or glowing. It names a physical source of heat and fire rather than an action or quality. The word occurs 29 times in the Greek LXX corpus, across passages from Genesis through Sirach, and its plural forms can refer to multiple burning coals. Its central meaning remains consistent wherever it appears: a coal still carrying fire. The surrounding verse determines how that image functions in a particular passage.

Antiochus is a personal name, referring to a particular man rather than expressing a general quality or action. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it appears 46 times, especially in 1, 2, 3, and 4 Maccabees. The name is used for historical figures in those books, but the bare name alone does not explain which Antiochus is intended in every passage. The surrounding verse and passage identify the person and clarify what is being said about him.

The verb means “fight from,” expressing fighting that proceeds from a stated place or position. It focuses on the action of fighting together with the idea of where that action begins or proceeds, rather than giving a broader description of the conflict. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, at 2 Maccabees 12:27. Its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse text.

This Greek LXX noun means “blinding,” referring to the act or condition of causing someone to lose sight or preventing clear vision. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament represented by the LXX, in Zechariah 12:4. The word’s precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains the removal or impairment of sight. It is a focused term rather than a broad word for confusion or difficulty.

Asimouth, also rendered Asimuth, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Ezekiel 25:9. The available information identifies the name but does not provide enough surrounding verse text to explain whom or what it designates there. Its meaning in that passage therefore depends on the actual context of Ezekiel 25:9, while its basic lexical function is simply to identify a named person, place, or other entity.

Atous, also rendered Atus, is a proper name rather than a word that describes an action, quality, or object. It identifies a person named in the Greek Old Testament. The name occurs three times in the LXX, appearing once in Ezra and twice in Nehemiah. Without the surrounding verse text, its specific role in each genealogy or list cannot be described further, but its basic meaning is the personal name Atous or Atus.

Apheka, also rendered Afeka, is a proper name for a place. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in 1 Kings 21:26 and 1 Kings 21:30. The word itself identifies the place rather than describing an action, quality, or person. Its precise significance in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and narrative context, but its basic lexical function is simply to name Apheka or Afeka.

This adjective means “unsuitable”—describing something that is not fit for a particular purpose, use, or situation. It identifies a person or thing as failing to meet what is needed or appropriate. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek biblical writings represented here, it occurs 10 times, with most occurrences in the deuterocanonical books. Its precise force in any verse depends on what person or thing is being described.

βαδίζω means “proceed”: it describes the action of moving onward or continuing on a journey. As a verb, it normally expresses what someone does rather than naming a person, place, or object. This LXX word occurs 56 times, making it a recurring action word rather than a rare expression. Its precise force in any particular verse comes from the surrounding sentence.

This word means “purse,” referring to a small container used to carry money. It is a noun describing an ordinary possession rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, once in Job and once in Proverbs. The word’s basic sense remains simple and concrete: a purse or money bag. The surrounding verse is needed to explain how the purse functions in either passage, but the word itself identifies the container.

This word means “bramble bush,” a noun naming a thorny or tangled shrub. In the Greek Old Testament, it refers to a bush or bramble rather than expressing an action or quality. It occurs seven times, including several times in Exodus 3 and once each in Deuteronomy 33:16 and Job 31:40. The precise significance of the plant in any particular passage comes from the surrounding verse and context.

This word is a proper name rendered “Bēthabara” or “Vithavara.” It identifies a specific named location in the Greek Old Testament rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. It occurs once in the LXX, at Joshua 18:22. Since the available information gives the name but not the surrounding verse text, its exact location and significance must be understood from that passage’s context.

This adjective means “edible”: something suitable or safe to be eaten. It describes food or produce according to whether it can be consumed. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears three times, in Leviticus, Nehemiah, and Ezekiel, so its basic sense remains consistent across these passages. The word identifies the quality of being fit for eating rather than naming a particular food or expressing an action. Its exact force in any verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

Gesiōngaber, also rendered Yesiongaver, is a proper name identifying a particular named place or location rather than describing an action, quality, or object in general. As a name, it is not normally translated by an ordinary meaning-word; its function is to identify the same place wherever it appears. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Numbers 33, in the itinerary record of Israel’s wilderness journey.

This Greek Old Testament verb means “make known” or “point out.” It describes the act of bringing something to someone’s attention so it becomes understood or recognized. Depending on the sentence, it can refer to revealing information, identifying something, or directing attention to it. The word appears 47 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish writings represented in this corpus, so it is a regularly used word for communicating or indicating something. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on what is being made known or pointed out.

This noun means “setting,” referring generally to the placing or arranging of something. In the Greek LXX corpus, it appears once, in Sirach 45:11. Its basic sense identifies an act or result of setting something in position, though the precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse. The word is therefore best understood as a term for placement or arrangement, rather than as a description of a person, object, or emotion.

This verb means “keep muttering”—to continue voicing complaints or dissatisfaction. It describes repeated grumbling rather than a single passing remark. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs ten times, chiefly in Exodus and Numbers, where its use is associated with people continually expressing discontent. The word is also found once in Sirach, showing that its basic sense remains understandable beyond the Pentateuch. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This noun means “thirst,” the physical desire or need for water. It describes a condition people experience when they lack sufficient water, and it can be expressed as being thirsty or as thirst itself. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek biblical writings, it occurs 12 times, including passages from Exodus, Deuteronomy, Judges, Nehemiah, Isaiah, and Wisdom. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

This noun means a “present”: something given to another person. It names a bestowed offering rather than an action or description, so its exact significance comes from what is being given and the surrounding sentence. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs five times, including in Daniel, Wisdom, and Maccabees. The word is therefore uncommon in this corpus but has a clear, concrete sense of a present or bestowed item.

Eglom is a proper name identifying a person in the Greek Old Testament. It is rendered as “Eglom” and does not function as a general description, action, or quality. The name appears eight times in seven verses within the Greek Old Testament, once in Joshua and repeatedly in Judges. Its lexical meaning is therefore the personal name itself; understanding the person’s role or actions requires the wording and surrounding context of each passage.

This Greek LXX verb means “make peace”: to bring about peaceful relations rather than conflict. It describes an action, so it focuses on actively establishing peace, not merely experiencing a peaceful feeling. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Proverbs 10:10. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text and context, but its basic meaning remains the act of making peace.

This adjective means “selected to judge”: it describes a person chosen for the role of judging. The emphasis is on being selected for that responsibility, not merely on performing an act of judgment. As an adjective, it characterizes someone in relation to this judging role. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in Sirach 42:11. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

This verb means “embitter”: it describes making someone or something bitter. As an action word, it points to the act of causing bitterness rather than naming a person, object, or quality. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in Deuteronomy 32:16. The word’s precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the act of embittering.

This noun means “olive tree; olive,” referring either to the tree itself or to its fruit. It names a familiar cultivated tree and the olives associated with it. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 21 times, showing regular use for this plant and its produce. Its exact sense in a particular verse depends on whether the surrounding sentence speaks of the tree or the olive fruit.

This Greek LXX verb means “pull in,” describing the action of drawing someone or something inward. It functions as an action word rather than a name or description. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Proverbs 4:11. That single occurrence identifies its basic sense, while the surrounding verse would be needed to explain exactly what is being pulled in and how the action functions there.

This Greek LXX adverb describes an action done “honourably; gloriously”—in a way that displays dignity, esteem, or splendour. It tells how something is carried out rather than naming a person, object, or event. The word occurs nine times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, including Exodus, Daniel, and 1 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse comes from the action and surrounding sentence, but its central idea is conduct marked by honour or glory.

This verb means being “in great doubt.” As a verb, it describes a person who is deeply perplexed or uncertain, especially when facing a difficult situation. It expresses inward bewilderment rather than a simple question or momentary hesitation. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Psalm 87:16. The word’s exact force in that sentence depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its ordinary lexical sense is “in great doubt.”

This Greek LXX verb means “fall heavy upon” or “fall heavily.” It describes something coming down with weight or force, emphasizing the heaviness of the action rather than merely its occurrence. The word appears once in the Greek LXX, in Job 29:4, but the available information does not include the verse text, so its specific force there cannot be described further. Its basic sense remains an action that presses or descends heavily upon something.

This verb means “shine after,” describing light or brightness appearing afterward. It presents shining as something that follows another event, condition, or period rather than simply existing at the same time. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice: once in Isaiah and once in Wisdom. Its exact force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its central idea is the arrival or appearance of brightness after something else. [P03 identity; P03 occurrences]

This noun refers to something or someone “given as a name.” It describes a naming designation rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it occurs once, in Esther 8:12, so its ordinary sense is best kept focused on the fact that a person or thing bears a name assigned to it. The exact force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but the basic lexical idea remains the assignment of a name.

This adjective describes a person who is rebellious or perverse—someone marked by resistance to what is right or proper. Its central sense points to a defiant, morally wayward character rather than a simple mistake or passing weakness. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Deuteronomy 21:18, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. The word’s basic meaning remains clear: it identifies someone characterized by rebellion or perversity.

Esthie is a proper name, referring to a particular named individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Samuel 30:28. The available rendering preserves the name as “Esthie,” so its meaning is primarily identifying rather than descriptive. The surrounding verse would be needed to explain who this person was or what role the name has in that passage.

This adjective means “opportune”: suitable, well-timed, or occurring at the right moment. It describes something whose timing fits a particular need or purpose, rather than merely something that happens quickly or conveniently. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs five times, including in Psalms and 2–3 Maccabees. Its exact force in any verse depends on what event, action, or circumstance the surrounding sentence presents.

This adjective describes something “decent”—proper, respectable, or fitting in appearance or character. It can qualify a person or thing that is viewed as becoming or suitable rather than shameful or out of place. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, it occurs six times across six verses, including passages in 2 Samuel, Job, Zechariah, Wisdom, and Sirach. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding wording.

This Greek LXX adverb means “clearly” or “distinctly.” It describes speech, understanding, or communication that is plain and unmistakable rather than vague or difficult to recognize. The word appears once in the Greek Old Testament text represented here, in Daniel 2:19. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its normal meaning emphasizes clarity: something is made known in a way that can be plainly perceived or understood.

Zakchou; Zakkhu is a proper name identifying a person in the Greek Old Testament. It is not a common word describing an object, action, quality, or idea, so its meaning is primarily the individual’s name rather than a broader concept. This name appears twice in the LXX corpus, once in Ezra 2:9 and once in Nehemiah 7:14. The available information identifies the name itself but does not provide further details about the person or the significance of the name.

“Iegebal; Ieyeval” is a proper name, identifying a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at Judges 8:11. Since the available information gives the name but not its meaning or a verse translation, the safest understanding is simply that it functions as a personal name in that passage. Its precise significance there depends on the surrounding verse and passage context.

This Greek LXX adjective means “cheerful,” describing a person or expression marked by gladness and a positive spirit. It can describe someone’s outward manner or emotional character rather than an action itself. The word occurs six times in the Greek LXX, appearing in Esther, Proverbs, Sirach, and 3 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central sense remains a cheerful or glad disposition.

This word is a proper name, referring to a person named “Iōphalēt,” also rendered “Iofalit.” It is not a general description, action, or quality, but a personal designation in the Greek Septuagint. The name occurs once in the LXX corpus, at 1 Chronicles 12:3. Without the surrounding verse text, Scripture does not provide enough here to explain more about the person or the specific role connected with the name.

This word means “small cord,” referring to a narrow, flexible cord or tie. It is a noun naming a physical object rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs four times, all in Judges, where its references are Judges 15:13–14 and 16:11–12. Its precise significance in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary meaning remains a small cord used as a binding or fastening material.

Kasia is a proper name. It identifies a person or designation rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs twice, once in Psalms and once in Ezekiel. Because the available information does not include the surrounding verse text, it does not establish the identity, character, or role of the person named. The word’s basic meaning is therefore simply “Kasia,” functioning as a personal name within these two Old Testament occurrences.

This verb means to applaud excessively—to respond with unusually intense or prolonged applause. It describes an action rather than a person, feeling, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Jeremiah 27:15. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself centers on excessive applause or enthusiastic clapping, not ordinary approval. The term is therefore best understood as an emphatic expression of praise through applause.

This verb means “reconcile”: to restore agreement or peace between parties who are at odds. It describes an action, not merely a condition, pointing to the process of bringing people or sides back into harmony. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs four times—once in Jeremiah and three times in 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in any one verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage, but its central idea remains the restoration of peaceful relationship.

This Greek LXX verb means “cover with mail,” referring to protecting someone or something with linked metal armor. It is a specialized action word rather than a general term for covering. The word appears once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 1 Maccabees 6:38. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, its precise force in that sentence cannot be described further, but its basic meaning points to armor used as protective covering.

This Greek LXX verb means “strike with thunderbolts,” describing the action of hitting or attacking with thunderbolts. It expresses an action rather than a person, object, or quality. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament tradition represented here, in Isaiah 30:30. Its precise force in that verse is determined by the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the striking action itself.

The word means “care” or “solicitude”—thoughtful concern directed toward another person or matter. It is a noun, naming an attitude or practice of attentive concern rather than an action word. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice, both times in 4 Maccabees. Its basic sense remains focused on careful regard or concern; the surrounding verse is needed to show exactly who or what receives that care.

This adjective describes something light in weight or movement, and therefore nimble or quick to move. It can portray physical agility, ease, or a lack of heaviness rather than a fixed object or person. In the Greek Old Testament and related LXX books, it occurs 18 times, including uses rendered “light” and “nimble.” Its precise force in any particular sentence depends on what is being described, but the central idea remains lightness that enables quick or agile movement.

This verb means to “desert one’s post,” describing someone abandoning an assigned position or duty rather than remaining where they are expected to serve. It presents desertion as an act of leaving one’s station. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 9:23. The surrounding verse is needed to explain the specific situation, but the word itself centers on abandoning one’s appointed post or responsibility.

Lobon, also rendered Lovon, is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies a named person or place rather than describing an action, quality, or object, although the available information does not specify which. The name occurs 20 times in 20 Old Testament verses, most often in Leviticus, with additional occurrences in Exodus, Deuteronomy, and Amos. Its precise referent must therefore be determined from the surrounding passage in each occurrence.

This word is a proper name, rendered as “Massalēm; Massalim.” It identifies a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 9:8. The available information establishes its name-like function and its single occurrence, but the verse reference by itself does not provide enough surrounding text to explain the person’s role or significance in that passage.

Melchiēli is a proper name, also rendered Melkhili. It identifies a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, at Numbers 26:29. The available lexical information gives the name itself but does not provide the surrounding verse text, so its specific family or narrative role cannot be described here. Its ordinary function is simply to identify the individual called Melchiēli in that passage.

This word means “from Tibhath,” identifying someone or something by connection with that place. It functions as a noun rather than expressing an action or quality. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 18:8. Since the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, the exact referent cannot be described further; the word’s supported sense is a designation of origin or association with Tibhath.

This Greek LXX noun means “pollution,” referring generally to something that makes a person or thing impure or defiled. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament translation, at Leviticus 13:44. The word itself identifies the condition of pollution, while the surrounding verse determines what is regarded as polluted in that passage. Its meaning is therefore centered on impurity or defilement rather than on a particular action or object.

This Greek LXX word means “friend,” describing a person who is associated with or favorably disposed toward someone else. It functions as a noun or adjective, so it can identify a companion or describe someone as friendly. In the Greek LXX, it occurs three times, all in Genesis. Its basic sense is relational: a person connected to another through friendship or companionship, rather than an abstract quality or action. The surrounding verse determines the precise nuance in each occurrence.

This adjective describes someone as “slow of mind” or “stupid.” It points to dullness in understanding or mental sluggishness, rather than describing a physical condition. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Proverbs 12:8. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic sense identifies a person whose thinking is noticeably dull or lacking sound judgment.

This word means a tooth, the hard part of the mouth used for biting and chewing. It is a noun referring to an individual tooth or, in context, teeth collectively. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 182 times, showing regular use for this literal bodily part. Scripture also uses teeth in figurative expressions, but the word itself retains its basic meaning; the surrounding verse determines whether a particular reference is literal or figurative.

Onnam is a personal name in the Greek Old Testament, identifying an individual rather than describing an action, quality, object, or spiritual concept. It appears once in the LXX corpus, in Joshua 18:16. Because the available biblical text and surrounding passage are not included here, the name itself does not establish the person’s identity, role, or significance. Its basic meaning is therefore simply the proper name Onnam.

Ulames is a proper name, referring to a person or place identified by that name. It is rendered as “Oulamais” or “Ulames,” preserving the name rather than describing an ordinary quality, action, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, at Judges 18:29. The name’s precise referent and significance depend on the surrounding passage, but the word itself functions as a distinctive proper name.

This word is a proper name, referring to a person named Uria, also rendered Ouria. It functions as a personal name rather than a general word describing an object, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs six times, across 2 Samuel, 2 Kings, Ezra, and Nehemiah. The name appears in passages belonging to different periods of Israel’s history, so its precise referent is determined by each passage. The name itself carries the identification, not a general definition for ordinary speech.

This noun refers to “juxta-position” or “neighbourhood”—things placed beside one another or situated close together. It can describe physical closeness, an arrangement of items, or the condition of being side by side. The word occurs eight times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, across historical and wisdom books. Its precise force in any verse depends on what people, objects, or places are being set beside one another.

This word means “axe,” the noun for a cutting tool. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice: once in Jeremiah 23:29 and once in Ezekiel 9:2. Its basic meaning remains concrete and straightforward, identifying the tool itself rather than an action or quality. The surrounding wording determines how the axe functions in each passage, but the word’s ordinary lexical sense is clear.

This Greek LXX word means “throwing stones.” It is a noun or adjective describing someone or something connected with casting stones, or the act and capability of doing so. The word occurs five times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish Scripture, including passages in 1 Samuel, Job, Ezekiel, and Wisdom. Its basic sense is concrete and action-focused: stones are being thrown, or a person or thing is characterized by that activity. The surrounding verse determines whether it functions as a description of an agent, an object, or an action.

This noun refers to broidered material or brocade—decorative cloth made with varied or ornamental stitching. It names a kind of richly worked fabric rather than an action or personal quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, in Jeremiah and Ezekiel, where its precise reference depends on the surrounding passage. The word therefore points to clothing or textile goods distinguished by elaborate design and craftsmanship.

This word refers to a drink or a draught—the liquid consumed or served for drinking. As a noun, it can name a beverage itself; as an adjective, it can describe something associated with drinking. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, it occurs 25 times, showing ordinary use for drink in settings involving meals, hospitality, vessels, or provisions. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding context.

This noun means “ancestor,” referring to someone from whom a person or family comes. It points backward to an earlier generation or forefather, whether considered individually or as a group. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 11 times, including passages in Esther, Sirach, and the Maccabean books. Its precise reference in any particular verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central sense remains a predecessor in one’s family line.

This adjective describes someone who is ready, willing, or eager to act. It can point to a person who is mentally prepared and favorably disposed toward a task, response, or course of action. The central idea is active readiness rather than reluctance: the person is inclined to respond or participate. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs six times, in both Old Testament and deuterocanonical books. Its precise emphasis in any passage depends on what the person is ready or eager to do.

This Greek LXX verb means to “persist” or “devote” oneself—to continue faithfully and give steady attention to a person, task, or purpose. It describes deliberate perseverance rather than a brief or occasional effort. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Numbers 13:20. The surrounding verse is needed to determine exactly what the person is devoted to there, but the word itself emphasizes continuing with firmness and dedication.

This Greek LXX verb means “push to,” describing an action that moves or presses someone or something toward a destination or object. It functions as a verb, so it expresses an act rather than a person, thing, or quality. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 2 Maccabees 13:6. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is the act of pushing toward something.

This adjective means “winged,” describing a creature or thing that has wings. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used six times across six verses, including descriptions associated with living creatures, animals, and flying things. Its basic function is to identify something by its possession or use of wings, rather than to name a particular species. The exact force in any verse depends on the noun it describes and the surrounding sentence.

Salim is a proper name, presented as the name “Salim” rather than as a common word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek LXX corpus, it appears once, at Joshua 19:22. Since the available information identifies the name but does not provide the surrounding verse text, it does not establish whether Salim refers to a person, settlement, or another named place in that passage. Its exact reference is Joshua 19:22.

Sebama is a proper name, also rendered Sevama, used for a named location in the Greek Old Testament. It is not a general word describing an action, quality, or object, but a particular name preserved in the biblical text. This name occurs five times in the Greek Old Testament, in Numbers, Joshua, and Isaiah. The English rendering consistently gives Sebama, while Sevama reflects the alternate form supplied for the same name.

This Greek LXX verb means “harden”: to make something firm, resistant, or unyielding, or to describe it becoming that way. Its basic sense concerns a change toward hardness rather than softness or responsiveness. The word occurs 35 times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, with especially frequent use in Exodus. Its exact force in any passage depends on who or what is being hardened and the surrounding sentence.

This verb means to prove barren or childless. It describes the condition of a person who does not bear children, with emphasis on barrenness rather than on a broader lack or deficiency. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Sirach 42:10. Its precise force in that passage is understood through the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic meaning is the inability to have children.

This Greek LXX verb means “collect”: to gather things or people together. It describes the act of bringing separate items into one group or place, whether the gathering is deliberate or happens as people respond to a situation. The word appears 39 times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX corpus, showing a broad everyday use for gathering.
